animal_models:
- name: Ganglionic alpha-synuclein fibril injection in TgM83 mice
  species: Mouse
  genotype: TgM83+/- (human SNCA A53T transgene, hemizygous)
  description: >-
    Preformed alpha-synuclein fibrils injected into the stellate and celiac ganglia
    of TgM83 mice spread only along autonomic pathways, to the central nervous system
    and bidirectionally to the autonomic innervation of peripheral organs. The mice
    develop orthostatic hypotension, constipation, hypohidrosis and hyposmia without
    motor dysfunction.
  publication: PMID:32071315
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Peripheral Autonomic Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation
    relationship: PARTIALLY_RECAPITULATES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    model_scale: ORGANISM
    description: >-
      Autonomic-restricted alpha-synuclein pathology with autonomic failure and no
      motor signs, the defining features of PAF.
    limitations: >-
      Pathology is seeded by injected fibrils into mice overexpressing mutant human
      alpha-synuclein, whereas human PAF is sporadic with no SNCA variant, and the
      seeded pathology also reaches the central nervous system.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: CAUSE_UNREPRESENTED
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        Aggregation is started by injecting preformed fibrils into ganglia of mice
        overexpressing A53T human alpha-synuclein. In the sporadic human disease the
        protein is wild type at normal dosage and the initiating trigger is unknown,
        so the model cannot speak to why aggregation begins.
    - divergence_type: SPECIES_MISMATCH
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        Orthostatic hypotension and hypohidrosis are measured in mice, whose
        postural cardiovascular load differs greatly from upright humans.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:32071315
      reference_title: "Autonomic ganglionic injection of α-synuclein fibrils as a model of pure autonomic failure α-synucleinopathy."
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: "In parallel, the mice develop autonomic dysfunction, featured by orthostatic hypotension, constipation, hypohidrosis and hyposmia, without motor dysfunction."
      explanation: The model reproduces autonomic failure without motor features.
  - target: Spread to Central Nervous System (Phenoconversion)
    relationship: PARTIALLY_RECAPITULATES
    fidelity: LOW
    model_scale: ORGANISM
    description: Pathology spreads from autonomic ganglia to the central nervous system.
    limitations: >-
      Central spread was shown histologically without the motor or cognitive
      phenotype of a phenoconverted disease, and the model has not been shown to
      separate Lewy-type from MSA-type conversion.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: PROXY_QUANTITY
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The model's quantity is the histological presence of alpha-synuclein pathology
        in central regions. The node's quantity is clinical phenoconversion to
        Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, which is a diagnosis made on
        motor or cognitive features the mice never develop. Central pathology stands in
        for a clinical event, and the proportion of PAF patients with central pathology
        who would ever convert is not something this model can report.
    - divergence_type: CAUSE_UNREPRESENTED
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        Spread is initiated by synthetic preformed fibrils in a host overexpressing A53T
        human alpha-synuclein. Aggregates purified from human sympathetic ganglia have
        failed to seed pathology in mouse brain, so whether the human peripheral
        aggregate propagates as this model's fibrils do is unsettled; see the
        paf_peripheral_aggregate_seeding_mismatch discussion.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:32071315
      reference_title: "Autonomic ganglionic injection of α-synuclein fibrils as a model of pure autonomic failure α-synucleinopathy."
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      snippet: "induces spreading of α-Syn pathology only through the autonomic pathway to both the central nervous system (CNS) and the autonomic innervation of peripheral organs bidirectionally"
      explanation: Autonomic-to-central spread of seeded pathology.
experimental_models:
- name: DOPAL challenge in BE(2)-M17 neuroblastoma cells and primary cortical neurons
  experimental_model_type: CELL_LINE
  organism:
    preferred_term: human
    term:
      id: NCBITaxon:9606
      label: Homo sapiens
  cell_source: >-
    Human BE(2)-M17 neuroblastoma cells overexpressing mCherry-tagged alpha-synuclein,
    with mouse primary cortical neurons carrying only endogenous alpha-synuclein as the
    non-overexpressing comparison, both exposed to exogenous DOPAL. HEK293T cells
    overexpressing alpha-synuclein-EGFP are the paper's negative arm: they supply the
    mass-spectrometric characterisation of the modified protein, but oligomers were not
    detected in them. An isolated synaptic-vesicle preparation is assayed alongside the
    intact cells.
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: BE(2)-M17 neuroblastoma cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000031
      label: neuroblast (sensu Vertebrata)
  - preferred_term: mouse primary cortical neuron
    term:
      id: CL:0000540
      label: neuron
  conditions:
  - Exogenous DOPAL exposure at 20 and 50 micromolar in the mouse primary neurons
  - Exogenous DOPAL exposure at 100 micromolar in the human overexpressing lines
  - Preformed alpha-synuclein-DOPAL oligomers at 2 micromolar for the cellular
    permeabilisation experiments
  - Alpha-synuclein overexpression, and endogenous alpha-synuclein alone
  culture_system: Two-dimensional monolayer culture, with an accompanying isolated synaptic-vesicle
    preparation
  publication: PMID:28084443
  description: >-
    The non-animal system behind the catecholaldehyde step of this entry. DOPAL added to
    the medium forms covalent oligomers with alpha-synuclein inside the cell, and those
    oligomers permeabilise cholesterol-containing membranes, damage synaptic vesicles and
    let dopamine escape into the cytoplasm, where it is converted to more DOPAL. It is
    the experiment that makes the vicious cycle drawn in this entry's pathograph
    measurable rather than inferred, and it works on endogenous as well as overexpressed
    alpha-synuclein. It is not a model of PAF. The cells are a neuroblastoma line and
    mouse cortical neurons rather than sympathetic noradrenergic neurons, no patient
    material is involved, and the catecholamine that leaks is dopamine rather than
    norepinephrine.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28084443
    reference_title: DOPAL derived alpha-synuclein oligomers impair synaptic vesicles physiological
      function.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    snippet: DOPAL can target both overexpressed aS and endogenous aS, and it is able to
      induce aS oligomerization in immortalized cell lines, and in primary neurons
    explanation: >-
      Establishes the system and that the effect does not depend on overexpression, which
      is what makes it usable as evidence about an endogenous mechanism.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Catecholaldehyde (DOPAL) Autotoxicity in Noradrenergic Neurons
    relationship: PERTURBS
    fidelity: MODERATE
    model_scale: MOLECULAR
    description: >-
      DOPAL is applied to intact cells and the covalent alpha-synuclein oligomers this
      node describes are then recovered from inside them, so the node's chemistry is
      demonstrated in a cellular context rather than only in a tube.
    limitations: >-
      DOPAL is supplied from outside at fixed concentrations, so the node's claim that it
      accumulates because dopamine leaks from storage vesicles and is deaminated in the
      cytoplasm is assumed by the design rather than tested by it.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: CAUSE_UNREPRESENTED
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The node's upstream cause is vesicular leak followed by monoamine oxidase
        deamination of cytoplasmic dopamine. Here the aldehyde is pipetted into the
        medium, so neither the leak nor the enzymatic step is in the model, and the
        exposure cannot be titrated to a physiological cytoplasmic concentration.
    - divergence_type: BOUNDARY_OMISSION
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        A sympathetic noradrenergic neuron is outside the model. Its distinguishing
        features - dopamine beta-hydroxylase inside the vesicle, norepinephrine rather
        than dopamine as the stored transmitter, and the aldehyde dehydrogenase
        complement of that cell type - are exactly what the node invokes to explain why
        catecholaminergic neurons are selectively affected.
    - divergence_type: SPECIES_MISMATCH
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The non-overexpressing arm uses mouse cortical neurons, and the species gap bears
        on this link because the endogenous-alpha-synuclein claim rests on that arm alone.
        Both human lines overexpress a tagged construct, and in the HEK293T line no
        oligomers were detected at all, so there is no human result showing the reaction
        on endogenous protein at endogenous abundance. The substrate in the neurons is the
        mouse protein rather than the human one, and those neurons were exposed to 20 or
        50 micromolar DOPAL against 100 micromolar in the human lines, so the two arms are
        not interchangeable on dose either.
    readouts:
    - name: Covalent alpha-synuclein oligomer formation after DOPAL exposure
      target: Catecholaldehyde (DOPAL) Autotoxicity in Noradrenergic Neurons
      direction: INCREASED
      interpretation: >-
        Oligomeric alpha-synuclein species appear on western blot in DOPAL-treated cells
        and not in untreated ones, in both the overexpressing line and neurons carrying
        only endogenous protein.
      evidence:
      - reference: PMID:28084443
        reference_title: DOPAL derived alpha-synuclein oligomers impair synaptic vesicles
          physiological function.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: IN_VITRO
        quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
        snippet: is able to induce aS oligomerization in immortalized cell lines, and in
          primary neurons
        explanation: The measurement behind this readout, in both cell systems.
  - target: Noradrenergic Vesicular Storage and Synthesis Defect
    relationship: PARTIALLY_RECAPITULATES
    fidelity: LOW
    model_scale: CELLULAR
    description: >-
      Catecholamine escaping from storage vesicles is the quantity this node is about, and
      it is measured here as a consequence of the aldehyde-driven oligomers rather than
      assumed. That is the return arm of the loop this entry draws between the storage
      defect and the catecholaldehyde node.
    limitations: >-
      The transmitter that leaks is dopamine from a neuroblastoma line and from cortical
      neurons, not norepinephrine from a sympathetic neuron, and vesicular monoamine
      transporter density and tyrosine hydroxylase content - the two measurements that
      define this node in patients - are not reported.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: PROXY_QUANTITY
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        Dopamine leak from synaptic vesicles stands in for failure of norepinephrine
        sequestration in a sympathetic varicosity. The direction of the defect is the
        same; the transmitter, the vesicle population and the cell are not.
    - divergence_type: BOUNDARY_OMISSION
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        Dopamine beta-hydroxylase and the noradrenergic vesicle itself lie outside the
        model, so nothing here bears on the reduced vesicular norepinephrine synthesis
        that this node also asserts.
    - divergence_type: SPECIES_MISMATCH
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The in-cell evidence that oligomers damage synaptic vesicles is the electron
        microscopy of mouse primary neurons, where the readily releasable pool shrinks and
        vesicles per synapse fall from about 71 to 49 and 38 with rising DOPAL. The human
        arm contributes the pHluorin permeabilisation result and the dopamine-leak assay
        is cell-free, so the structural measurement of vesicle loss has no human
        counterpart here.
    readouts:
    - name: Dopamine leak from synaptic vesicles
      target: Noradrenergic Vesicular Storage and Synthesis Defect
      direction: INCREASED
      interpretation: >-
        Alpha-synuclein-DOPAL oligomers permeabilise vesicle membranes and release stored
        dopamine, in isolated vesicles and in cells.
      evidence:
      - reference: PMID:28084443
        reference_title: DOPAL derived alpha-synuclein oligomers impair synaptic vesicles
          physiological function.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: IN_VITRO
        quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
        snippet: aS-DOPAL oligomers can induce dopamine leak in an in vitro model of synaptic
          vesicles and in cellular models
        explanation: The measured leak, which is the step that closes the loop back onto
          the aldehyde node.
      - reference: PMID:28084443
        reference_title: DOPAL derived alpha-synuclein oligomers impair synaptic vesicles
          physiological function.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: IN_VITRO
        quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
        snippet: DOPAL-induced aS oligomer formation in neurons is associated with damage
          of synaptic vesicles
        explanation: Ties the vesicle damage to the oligomers rather than to DOPAL exposure
          generally.
- name: MO3.13 oligodendrocyte and PC12 catecholaldehyde transfer co-culture
  experimental_model_type: CO_CULTURE
  organism:
    preferred_term: human
    term:
      id: NCBITaxon:9606
      label: Homo sapiens
  cell_source: >-
    Human MO3.13 oligodendrocyte and glioblastoma lines, which contain neither
    catecholamines nor alpha-synuclein of their own, co-incubated with
    dopamine-producing rat PC12 cells or exposed to DOPAL directly, with recombinant
    wild-type or A53T alpha-synuclein supplied in the medium.
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: MO3.13 oligodendrocyte
    term:
      id: CL:0000128
      label: oligodendrocyte
  - preferred_term: PC12 pheochromocytoma cell
    term:
      id: CL:0000166
      label: chromaffin cell
  conditions:
  - Co-incubation with dopamine-producing PC12 cells
  - Exogenous DOPAL exposure
  - Wild-type and A53T alpha-synuclein supplied extracellularly
  culture_system: Two-dimensional co-incubation of two cell lines in shared medium
  publication: PMID:26777075
  description: >-
    A catecholamine-free recipient cell used as a clean background for the aldehyde. It
    answers a question the single-cell systems cannot: whether DOPAL made in one cell
    reaches another and oligomerises alpha-synuclein there. It was built to explain glial
    inclusions in multiple system atrophy, so for PAF it bears on the chemistry and the
    transmissibility and not on the cell type, and the entry's other MO3.13 result on
    DOPAL-driven quinonisation of intracellular proteins comes from the same laboratory.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26777075
    reference_title: DOPAL is transmissible to and oligomerizes alpha-synuclein in human
      glial cells.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    snippet: DOPAL is transmissible to glial cells and enhances intracellular oligomerization
      of AS
    explanation: >-
      The system's own conclusion, and the reason it is recorded here rather than folded
      into the single-cell model above.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Catecholaldehyde (DOPAL) Autotoxicity in Noradrenergic Neurons
    relationship: PERTURBS
    fidelity: LOW
    model_scale: MOLECULAR
    description: >-
      Shows the aldehyde crossing from a catecholamine-synthesising cell into a recipient
      that makes none, and oligomerising alpha-synuclein once inside, so the oligomerising
      step this node asserts does not require the aldehyde to be made in the same cell.
    limitations: >-
      The recipient is a glial line chosen for the multiple system atrophy question, and
      neither alpha-synuclein nor the catecholamine is endogenous to it, so the model
      reproduces the reaction and not the cell in which this entry places it.
    divergences:
    - divergence_type: BOUNDARY_OMISSION
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        The sympathetic noradrenergic neuron is absent, and so is the intracellular origin
        of the aldehyde. Alpha-synuclein is added from outside rather than expressed, so
        the model cannot speak to the concentrations either species reaches in the
        affected neuron.
    - divergence_type: PROXY_QUANTITY
      materiality: QUALIFYING
      description: >-
        An oligodendrocyte taking up extracellular alpha-synuclein stands in for a
        peripheral noradrenergic neuron aggregating its own. The cell-type selectivity
        that this node exists to explain is therefore not something the model can test.
    - divergence_type: SPECIES_MISMATCH
      materiality: IMMATERIAL
      description: >-
        The dopamine-producing partner in the transfer arm is a rat PC12 line. Immaterial
        to the claim, because the arm with DOPAL added directly to the human cells gives
        the same result.
discussions:
- discussion_id: paf_what_initiates_aggregation
  prompt: >-
    What starts alpha-synuclein aggregating in peripheral autonomic neurons in PAF, and
    does the catecholaldehyde DOPAL accumulate in those neurons before the aggregates
    appear?
  kind: KNOWLEDGE_GAP
  status: OPEN
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#Catecholaldehyde (DOPAL) Autotoxicity in Noradrenergic Neurons
  - pathophysiology#Peripheral Autonomic Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation
  - mechanistic_hypotheses#catecholaldehyde_autotoxicity
  rationale: >-
    The entry's canonical chain begins at aggregation, and the aggregation node says the
    initiating trigger is unknown. The catecholaldehyde node upstream of it rests on
    cell-free chemistry, postmortem tissue from other Lewy body diseases and a
    computational model; nothing has measured DOPAL, aldehyde dehydrogenase activity or
    the DOPAC:DOPAL ratio in sympathetic tissue from patients with PAF. The gap matters
    for more than completeness, because the two interventions the hypothesis implies -
    inhibiting monoamine oxidase to make less DOPAL, and antioxidant treatment to stop
    its oxidation - are both available, and PAF is the one Lewy body disease where the
    affected neurons are accessible by skin and vein biopsy. The author of the
    hypothesis lists the PAF form of the question explicitly as unanswered.
  posed_by: "dismech curation (PR #15556)"

- discussion_id: paf_peripheral_aggregate_seeding_mismatch
  prompt: >-
    Can alpha-synuclein aggregates taken from human peripheral sympathetic ganglia
    actually seed and propagate pathology, as the mouse fibril-injection model of PAF
    assumes?
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  status: OPEN
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#Peripheral Autonomic Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation
  - pathophysiology#Spread to Central Nervous System (Phenoconversion)
  - animal_models#Mouse
  rationale: >-
    The animal model in this entry seeds pathology by injecting synthetic preformed
    fibrils into the ganglia of mice overexpressing mutant human alpha-synuclein, and
    the pathology then spreads along autonomic pathways into the central nervous
    system. That result is the main experimental support for the phenoconversion node.
    But when Lewy-body aggregates purified from the stellate ganglia of Parkinson
    disease patients were inoculated into mouse brain, they produced neither pathology
    nor degeneration, while aggregates from the same patients' substantia nigra did.
    So the seeding competence demonstrated in the model may be a property of synthetic
    fibrils in a transgenic host rather than of the human peripheral aggregate the
    model stands for. This is a mismatch rather than a missing experiment: evidence
    exists on both sides and points in opposite directions, and what is unresolved is
    whether the human peripheral aggregate propagates at all.

  posed_date: '2026-10-26T00:00:00Z'

  proposed_experiments:
  - experiment_id: paf_ganglion_aggregate_seeding_competence
    name: Seeding competence of PAF-derived ganglionic aggregates
    description: >-
      Purify alpha-synuclein aggregates from sympathetic ganglia of autopsy-confirmed
      PAF cases, rather than from Parkinson disease cases or from synthetic fibrils, and
      test them both in seed amplification assays and by inoculation into the ganglia of
      wild-type and TgM83 mice. The published negative result used Parkinson disease

- discussion_id: no_exposure_epidemiology
  kind: KNOWLEDGE_GAP
  attaches_to:
  - environmental#
  prompt: >-
    Has any environmental, occupational or lifestyle exposure been studied as a
    risk factor for pure autonomic failure?
  rationale: >-
    This entry carries no environmental section because no exposure study of
    this disease was found, not because exposures were judged irrelevant. A
    deep-research sweep of exposure epidemiology across the
    alpha-synucleinopathies returned substantial literature for Parkinson
    disease, a single unreplicated case-control study for multiple system
    atrophy, one multicentre case-control study for isolated REM sleep
    behaviour disorder and one for dementia with Lewy bodies, and nothing at
    all for this disease. The gap matters because the exposure findings that do
    exist do not agree with one another across these diseases: smoking is
    inversely associated with Parkinson disease, positively associated with
    isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder and null in dementia with Lewy
    bodies, and occupational pesticide exposure is positive in Parkinson
    disease and null in multiple system atrophy under a formal job-exposure
    matrix. Nothing can therefore be inferred about this disease from its
    neighbours, and an exposure profile for a condition whose pathology is
    largely restricted to the peripheral autonomic nervous system would bear
    directly on whether peripheral-onset disease has a distinct trigger.
  notes: >-
    Recorded as an absence of evidence rather than as evidence of absence. The
    searches run were disease-named exposure queries across the
    synucleinopathies; a dedicated search strategy for this disease, including
    its synonyms and the older Bradbury-Eggleston designation, has not been
    run and might surface case series that a cross-disease sweep missed.
notes: >-
  PAF is sporadic and has no causal gene; SNCA is recorded on pathophysiology nodes as
  the gene of the aggregating protein, not as a genetic cause. Rare pathogenic SNCA
  lesions (the E46K variant, gene triplication) can produce PAF or its cardiac
  noradrenergic lesion and are cited as indirect evidence on the aggregation node.

Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF): Research Report
claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-23T17:39:03.907495

Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF): Research Report

MONDO:0018608 · ORPHA:441 · MeSH D054970 · ICD-11 8D84 · ICD-10 G90.8 (Orphanet maps this as "Narrower") · UMLS C0393911 · GARD 10428 Report prepared 2026-10-23. Evidence comes from the abstracts and full texts already cached for this entry in references_cache/. Ontology CURIEs were checked against the repository's term caches (cache/*/terms.csv); terms that were not in the cache are marked "lookup needed".

1. Disease information

Overview

Pure autonomic failure (PAF) is a rare, sporadic, adult-onset neurodegenerative disease of the peripheral autonomic nervous system. It is classed as an α-synucleinopathy. Its defining feature is chronic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) with no identified secondary cause and no motor or cognitive signs of central neurodegeneration.

PAF has no causal gene, and no OMIM entry is recorded. It is not a Mendelian disease. Orphanet records its inheritance as "Not applicable". Its molecular substrate is aggregated α-synuclein, the protein encoded by SNCA (hgnc:11138). That makes SNCA the disease protein, not a germline causal gene, and this report found no source naming a PAF-specific variant.

  • Orphanet definition: "A rare sporadic neurodegenerative disease characterized by slowly progressive symptoms of orthostatic hypotension (OH), and other symptoms of generalised dysautonomia related to the impairment of the sympathetic component of the autonomic nervous system." (ORPHA:441)
  • "Pure autonomic failure (PAF) is a rare sporadic neurodegenerative autonomic disorder characterized by slowly progressive pan autonomic failure without other features of neurologic dysfunctions." (PMID:27338613, 2016 review)
  • Historical description: "A 1925 report by Bradbury and Eggleston first described patients with extreme orthostatic hypotension and a low, steady heart rate." (PMID:24095130)

Synonyms

Bradbury-Eggleston syndrome, idiopathic orthostatic hypotension, PAF, pure dysautonomia, and "pure idiopatic dysautonomia" (Orphanet's own spelling). Older literature also uses "asympathicotonic orthostatic hypotension" (PMID:34669076).

Nature of the data

Nearly all of the evidence is aggregated at the disease level: multicentre cohorts, single-centre retrospective series, autopsy case reports, and consensus statements. There are no EHR-derived phenotype profiles.

A conceptual caveat

PAF is diagnosed clinically, and autopsy and neurochemical data show that the clinical label covers two separate conditions (PMID:34669076, Goldstein 2021):

"This approach lumps together two nOH syndromes that are pathologically and neurochemically distinct. One is characterized by intraneuronal cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein aggregates (i.e., Lewy bodies) and degeneration of postganglionic sympathetic neurons, as in PD and DLB; the other is not, as in MSA."

One autopsied clinically diagnosed PAF case had no synuclein pathology anywhere (PMID:28188385):

"In pure autonomic failure, sympathetic noradrenergic denervation can occur without concurrent Lewy bodies or alpha-synuclein deposition in the brain or sympathetic ganglion tissue."

2. Etiology

Factor Evidence
Primary cause Idiopathic neurodegeneration with misfolded α-synuclein deposited mainly in peripheral autonomic neurons. "PAF is a peripheral autonomic neurodegenerative disease caused by alpha-synuclein deposition that is predominantly confined to peripheral autonomic neurons." (PMID:34392300)
Genetic risk No causal genes, susceptibility loci, or GWAS signals specific to PAF were found in the cached literature. Orphanet: inheritance "Not applicable".
Environmental risk None established. This report found no toxin, occupational, or infectious exposure linked to PAF.
Demographics Age is the main correlate: onset is in adulthood or old age. Men predominate in pooled data (63.8% male; PMID:42081229), although one small Stanford series was 63% female (PMID:27757562).
Protective factors None documented.
Gene–environment interaction No data.

The prion-like spreading model is the leading mechanistic hypothesis for the whole synucleinopathy family. It is cited as background in PMID:28093795: "α-Syn spreads from cell-to-cell in a 'prion-like fashion.'" No PAF-specific trigger has been identified.

3. Phenotypes

Onset is in adulthood. The course is chronic and slowly progressive, and repeat testing shows worsening autonomic failure over time (PMID:40397689).

Thermoregulatory dysfunction / heat intolerance HP:0002046 38% PMID:40053259

Aggravating factors and quality of life. "Postural symptoms (mainly dizziness and neck pain) were worse in the morning and with warm temperature, straining, exertion, arm movements and food ingestion" (PMID:10552235). Compensatory palpitations and sweating were absent. Patients may only be able to stand for minutes at a time (PMID:21664375; PMID:25185131). Falls and syncope drive disability (PMID:33705537).

4. Genetic and molecular information

  • Causal genes: none. This is a sporadic, non-Mendelian disease.
  • Disease protein: α-synuclein (SNCA, hgnc:11138), present as phosphorylated or misfolded aggregates. CSF α-syn seeding assays (PMCA) are positive in 94% of PAF patients (PMID:33881777).
  • Molecular deficits in noradrenergic terminals. Forearm vein biopsies show "normal abundance of the NE transporter (NET) protein, together with very low levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)... and reduced vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2)" (PMID:29162745). The relevant genes are TH (hgnc:11782), SLC18A2/VMAT2 (lookup needed), and SLC6A2/NET (hgnc:11048).
  • Variants, allele frequencies, ClinVar entries, modifiers, epigenetics, chromosomal abnormalities: none reported in the sources reviewed. No ClinGen gene–disease validity applies.

5. Environmental information

No established environmental, lifestyle, or infectious cause. Factors that aggravate symptoms (not causes) are heat, meals, straining, exertion, and vasoactive drugs such as alpha-blockers (PMID:10552235; PMID:32979782; PMID:28717053).

6. Mechanism and pathophysiology

Ordered causal chain

  1. Initiating event (unknown). α-Synuclein misfolds and aggregates in peripheral autonomic neurons. The trigger is unknown, and prion-like spread is a hypothesis carried over from the synucleinopathy literature rather than something shown in PAF.
  2. This leads to Lewy bodies and neurites in sympathetic ganglia and distal autonomic axons, and degeneration of preganglionic intermediolateral-column neurons and postganglionic sympathetic neurons. PMID:9255396: "histopathologically by cell loss in intermediolateral columns and sympathetic ganglia"; Lewy bodies were found "in sympathetic ganglia, as well as in autonomic axons in the epicardial fat... and autonomic nerves in the muscularis of the urinary bladder." PMID:27338613: "neuronal degeneration of pre- and postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons in the thoracic spinal cord and paravertebral autonomic ganglia."
  3. Branch: the non-Lewy form, a preganglionic lesion only, carries a risk of premotor MSA (PMID:34669076).
  4. This results in postganglionic noradrenergic denervation plus a vesicular storage defect in the surviving nerves. "PAF entails moderately decreased cardiac sympathetic innervation and a substantial vesicular storage defect in residual nerves" (PMID:32945121). Denervation is widespread, affecting the heart and renal cortex (PMID:16269589), and skin, where p-syn is found "in the postganglionic sympathetic adrenergic and cholinergic nerve fibers" (PMID:23390175).
  5. This leads to failure of norepinephrine synthesis and release. TH is low and VMAT2 reduced (PMID:29162745). The lesions "are responsible for defects in the synthesis and release of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals, resulting in significant hypotension" (PMID:28717053). Plasma NE is very low.
  6. This results in failed baroreflex-mediated vasoconstriction on standing, giving neurogenic OH with a blunted heart-rate response (ΔHR/ΔSBP < 0.5 bpm/mmHg; PMID:29405350). Peripheral resistance is not maintained. PMID:39608812 infers that "P-syn deposition on autonomic nerves may impair control of total peripheral resistance giving rise to symptomatic orthostatic hypotension."
  7. Cerebral and muscle hypoperfusion follow, producing syncope, dizziness, visual disturbance, and coat-hanger pain (PMID:10552235).
  8. Parallel branches from denervation:
  9. Denervation supersensitivity of β-adrenoceptors and pressor sensitivity: "supersensitivity of cardiac beta-adrenoreceptors" (PMID:18514012). This underlies exaggerated responses to pressor drugs and to the water-drinking osmopressor reflex (PMID:21048076).
  10. Supine hypertension. The mechanism is incompletely understood. Plasma renin is suppressed, but angiotensin II is elevated and mineralocorticoid receptors are activated (PMID:26644241). Supine hypertension then drives nocturnal pressure natriuresis, which leads to volume depletion and worse morning OH (PMID:11927799), and also LVH.
  11. Loss of sympathetic drive to erythropoiesis, giving low erythropoietin and anemia (PMID:8017744; the authors' hypothesis is that "the sympathetic nervous system stimulates erythropoiesis").
  12. Sudomotor, bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction from involvement of the cholinergic sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways.
  13. Central spread in a subset (phenoconversion). Nigral dopaminergic loss is already present: "PAF and PD entail similarly severe nigral and overall central dopaminergic denervation," with the striatum relatively spared (PMID:18363034). Neuromelanin MRI shows loss in the locus ceruleus and substantia nigra in high-risk PAF (PMID:39825743). Hyposmia and RBD are central markers. Progression leads to PD, DLB, or MSA (see §8).

Checklist mapping

  • Cell types (cache-verified CL): sympathetic neuron CL:0011103; noradrenergic neuron CL:0008025; cholinergic neuron CL:0000108; dopaminergic neuron CL:0000700. A preganglionic neuron term needs lookup.
  • Processes (GO terms still need lookup; none were verified here): norepinephrine biosynthesis, catecholamine secretion and storage (vesicular monoamine transport), protein aggregation, baroreflex blood-pressure regulation, neuron death.
  • Chemicals (CHEBI): noradrenaline CHEBI:33569.
  • Immune involvement: none described.
  • Molecular profiling: no transcriptomic, proteomic, or single-cell PAF datasets were found in the cached sources. CSF NfL is elevated only in patients who later convert to MSA (PMID:33881777).

7. Anatomical structures affected

  • Primary: the peripheral autonomic nervous system. This means the sympathetic ganglia (UBERON term lookup needed), the thoracic intermediolateral column, and postganglionic fibres.
  • End organs (UBERON, cache-verified): heart UBERON:0000948 (cardiac denervation); kidney UBERON:0002113 (renal cortex); skin of body UBERON:0002097 and sweat gland UBERON:0001820; urinary bladder (lookup needed).
  • Central nervous system (subclinical or in converters): substantia nigra UBERON:0002038 and locus ceruleus UBERON:0002148 (PMID:9255396; PMID:18363034; PMID:39825743).
  • Subcellular: neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions (Lewy bodies) and synaptic or secretory vesicles (the storage defect).
  • Distribution: symmetric and length-dependent, with small-fibre loss (PMID:26606657). In PAF, p-syn is found at every biopsy site: "the site of analysis is irrelevant in PAF."

8. Temporal development

  • Onset: insidious, in adulthood or old age. Pooled mean onset age is 63.1 ± 4.3 years (PMID:42081229). At enrollment in the US cohort, patients were 68 years old (median) and had had autonomic failure for 5 years (PMID:28093795). Most non-OH autonomic symptoms begin near OH onset, while RBD comes later (median 7 years; PMID:40053259).
  • Course: chronic and progressive, with no remission.
  • Phenoconversion (the central prognostic issue):
Study n Follow-up Converted Breakdown
US consortium (PMID:28093795) 74 ≤4 y 34% DLB 13, PD 6, MSA 6
Mayo retrospective (PMID:28202694) 78 assessable of 318 ≥3 y 12% of possible PAF MSA 22, PD/DLB 11
Mayo (PMID:32546656) 275 — 24% MSA 34, PD/DLB 33
8-centre prospective (PMID:38366572; NCT01799915) 149 mean 3 y 33% PD 42%, DLB 35%, MSA 23%; ~12% per year
Queen Square (PMID:40397689) 281 median 10 y 33% 53% of deaths still had the PAF phenotype
UK multimodal (PMID:40696849) 194 median 13 y 26% MSA or LBD
Meta-analysis (PMID:42081229) 900 (9 studies) 6.4 y 30% MSA 12%, DLB 11%, PD 7%; 5.09 per 100 person-years

The meta-analysis concludes that "PAF may be a prodromal presentation of PD, DLB, or MSA with phenoconversion incidence rates similar to those of RBD." MSA conversions cluster in the early years, while Lewy body conversions occur at a steady rate. Note that the annual-risk estimates differ: about 12% per year in PMID:38366572 against about 5% per year in the pooled analysis.

  • Critical window: the pre-motor phase is the opportunity for disease-modifying trials (PMID:37843677; PMID:42444112).

9. Inheritance and population

  • Inheritance: sporadic, not applicable (ORPHA:441). There is no penetrance, anticipation, founder effect, or carrier-frequency data.
  • Prevalence: Orphanet gives a point-prevalence class of 1–9 per 1,000,000 (Europe). The source field in that row reads "PMID:2007", which looks malformed and should be checked before citing. No population-based incidence study was found.
  • Sex: male predominance in pooled cohorts (63.8%; PMID:42081229). In the Queen Square cohort, male sex was associated with conversion to Lewy body disease (PMID:40397689).
  • Geography and ethnicity: no data. Cohorts are mainly from the US and UK.

10. Diagnostics

Clinical criteria. OH is defined as a sustained fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic blood pressure within 3 minutes of standing or tilt (consensus statement, PMID:21431947). PAF additionally requires no secondary cause and no motor or cognitive CNS features (1996 consensus criteria, as cited in PMID:40696849). Neurogenic supine hypertension is defined as SBP ≥140 and/or DBP ≥90 mmHg after 5 minutes supine (PMID:29766366). Screening and treatment recommendations: PMID:28050656.

Test Finding in PAF Source
Tilt table / active stand nOH; ΔHR/ΔSBP < 0.492 bpm/mmHg (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 88.4%) PMID:29405350
Supine plasma norepinephrine Very low. Values >100 pg/mL (Mayo) or ≥200 pg/mL (UK, Queen Square) predict conversion PMID:28093795; PMID:28202694; PMID:40696849
Cardiac ¹⁸F-dopamine PET / ¹²³I-MIBG Denervated. MIBG abnormal in 84.6% of 39 cases. Low cardiac ¹⁸F-dopamine predicts conversion to LBD; normal uptake points toward MSA PMID:16269589; PMID:41072204; PMID:37843677
Skin biopsy for phosphorylated α-synuclein Positive in 100% (22 of 22) in Synuclein-One versus 3.3% of controls. A total p-syn score >3 separates PAF from MSA (specificity 100%, sensitivity 82%). Absent in acquired autonomic neuropathies PMID:38506839; PMID:39608812; PMID:23390175; PMID:26606657
Skin autonomic innervation, sympathetic skin responses Marked postganglionic denervation, whereas skin innervation is preserved in MSA PMID:20660924; PMID:18805037
CSF α-syn PMCA and NfL PMCA positive in 94%. An MSA-like seeding profile or raised NfL predicts MSA PMID:33881777
Autonomic reflex screen / thermoregulatory sweat test Moderate to severe failure. A preganglionic sweat-loss pattern predicts MSA PMID:40053259; PMID:28202694
Smell test (UPSIT) Hyposmia, which points toward PD/DLB conversion PMID:19201246; PMID:42081229
DaTSCAN, FDOPA-PET, neuromelanin MRI Abnormal DaTSCAN in 39% of patients up to 7 years before conversion PMID:40397689; PMID:39825743
Polysomnography RBD confirmation PMID:27757562
Pupillometry Sympathetic deficits. Normal pupils predict conversion PMID:40696849

Genetic testing: not indicated for PAF itself. It can be used to exclude mimics.

Differential diagnosis: prodromal MSA, PD or DLB with OH, autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy, amyloid and diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and non-neurogenic OH from volume depletion, anemia, or polypharmacy (PMID:34392300; PMID:29405350). The MDS prodromal-MSA criteria are 92–100% sensitive in PAF but only 56–67% specific. Requiring UPSIT >28 raises specificity to 90–97% (PMID:42444112).

Screening: no population or newborn screening exists.

11. Outcome and prognosis

  • Survival: median 15 years from orthostatic symptom onset, driven mainly by age and OH severity (PMID:40397689). In that cohort, 41% died during follow-up. Survival is better than in the other synucleinopathies (PMID:27338613; PMID:24095130).
  • Patients who stay "pure" have very low NE, a slow resting heart rate, no RBD, and preserved smell (PMID:28093795). "not all patients with pure autonomic failure will develop motor or cognitive symptoms, even with prolonged follow-up" (PMID:40053259).
  • Predictors of conversion to MSA: younger onset, severe bladder dysfunction, preserved smell, HR rise on tilt >10 bpm, higher NE, preganglionic anhidrosis, subtle motor signs, CSF NfL (PMID:28093795; PMID:38366572; PMID:33881777).
  • Predictors of conversion to PD/DLB: hyposmia, blunted tilt HR response (HR 6.1 for PD), RBD, low cardiac ¹⁸F-dopamine, male sex, older age (PMID:38366572; PMID:37843677; PMID:40397689).
  • Predictor of any conversion: RBD (odds ratio 7.1; PMID:28093795).
  • Complications: syncope, falls, injury, supine hypertension with end-organ damage (LVH, transient ischemic attack in one case series), anemia (PMID:15633433; PMID:11927799; PMID:8017744).

12. Treatment

There is no disease-modifying therapy: "There is currently no specific treatment to stop progression in PAF" (PMID:27338613). The goal of treatment is to relieve symptoms, not to normalize blood pressure (PMID:33705537).

Choosing a drug. Patients with low "sympathetic reserve", which includes PAF, "tend to respond better to 'norepinephrine replacers' (midodrine and droxidopa)" (PMID:32979782).

  • Pharmacogenomics: none described.
  • Gene, cell, and RNA therapies: none.
  • Trials: registered work is mostly observational, e.g., NCT01799915 (natural history) and NCT04700722 (Synuclein-One). Phenoconversion biomarkers are being developed specifically to select patients for future disease-modification trials (PMID:37843677; PMID:42444112).

13. Prevention

  • Primary prevention: none is possible, because the cause is unknown.
  • Secondary prevention: early detection through skin p-syn and autonomic testing, and stratifying conversion risk for trial enrollment.
  • Tertiary prevention: fall and syncope prevention through education about triggers and medications (PMID:33705537); treating supine hypertension to prevent LVH and nocturnal natriuresis (PMID:11927799; PMID:29766366).
  • Genetic counseling: not applicable, since PAF is sporadic.
  • Vaccination, public-health, and environmental measures: not applicable.

14. Other species and natural disease

No naturally occurring PAF in animals was found in the cached literature, and there is no relevant OMIA entry. Not applicable for transmission or zoonosis.

15. Model organisms

There is no dedicated PAF animal model in the reviewed sources.

  • Related models: sinoaortic-denervated mice, which model loss of baroreflex buffering, show the osmopressor response. Trpv4 is implicated in that response (PMID:21048076, review, MODEL_ORGANISM).
  • What a model would need to capture: a peripherally restricted synucleinopathy with postganglionic noradrenergic degeneration and spared striatum. The SNCA-based models of the wider synucleinopathy literature were not reviewed here, and none in the cached sources was shown to reproduce PAF specifically. This is a candidate KNOWLEDGE_GAP / HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH.

Notes for knowledge-base curation

  1. Lump/split: a single Disease entry seems right. Two candidate subtypes or hypotheses could be modelled: Lewy-body PAF (postganglionic, converts to PD/DLB) and non-Lewy PAF (preganglionic, possible premotor MSA) (PMID:34669076; PMID:28188385; PMID:37843677).
  2. Do not add genetic: causal genes. SNCA belongs on pathophysiology nodes (aggregation) as the disease protein.
  3. Wire every phenotype into the pathograph. OH should be the hub, with branches to cerebral hypoperfusion (syncope, dizziness, visual symptoms), muscle hypoperfusion (neck pain), supine hypertension → nocturia/LVH, and denervation → anemia.
  4. Conformance target: check just list-modules for an α-synuclein aggregation or autonomic module before adding one.
  5. CURIEs still to look up: HP terms for supine hypertension, dizziness, and postprandial hypotension; UBERON terms for sympathetic ganglion, intermediolateral column, and urinary bladder; a CL term for preganglionic neuron; all GO process terms; HGNC for SLC18A2.
  6. Orphanet epidemiology source: the "PMID:2007" source in the ORPHA:441 epidemiology row looks malformed. Do not cite it as a PMID.

Pure Autonomic Failure (MONDO:0018608) — Comprehensive Disease Characteristics Report
openscientist-autonomous 29 citations 2026-10-24T13:32:26.700060

Pure Autonomic Failure (MONDO:0018608) — Comprehensive Disease Characteristics Report

Summary

Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF; Bradbury–Eggleston syndrome) is a rare, sporadic, adult/late-onset peripheral α-synucleinopathy. It has no Mendelian causal gene; its central causal protein is α-synuclein, encoded by SNCA (HGNC:11138; chromosome 4q22.1), which misfolds and aggregates as Lewy-body-type neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions predominantly within the peripheral autonomic nervous system — postganglionic sympathetic neurons, sympathetic ganglia, the intermediolateral columns of the spinal cord, and distal autonomic axons of the heart and bladder. The resulting degeneration and biochemical dysfunction of noradrenergic neurons (tyrosine-hydroxylase depletion, impaired vesicular catecholamine storage, postganglionic denervation) produces a profound norepinephrine deficiency and the hallmark clinical feature of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH), together with genitourinary, gastrointestinal, and sudomotor autonomic failure. Although PAF is historically regarded as an isolated condition, it is now understood as a localized/prodromal synucleinopathy: approximately 30% of patients phenoconvert over ~6 years to a central synucleinopathy — multiple system atrophy (MSA), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), or Parkinson's disease (PD).

Diagnosis rests on autonomic function testing demonstrating neurogenic OH, low supine plasma norepinephrine without orthostatic rise, cutaneous phosphorylated α-synuclein on skin biopsy, CSF α-synuclein seed-amplification assays (αSyn-PMCA), and reduced cardiac sympathetic imaging (¹²³I-MIBG scintigraphy). There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is symptomatic and pathophysiology-guided — non-pharmacologic measures (salt/fluid loading, compression garments, physical counter-maneuvers, head-up sleeping) plus norepinephrine-replacing drugs (midodrine, droxidopa), which are preferred in PAF because of its low peripheral sympathetic reserve, balanced carefully against comorbid neurogenic supine hypertension.

This report synthesizes 11 confirmed findings and 37 reviewed papers across all 15 requested sections. The strongest, best-supported conclusions are: (1) PAF is molecularly an α-synucleinopathy with a peripheral noradrenergic lesion; (2) the biochemical signature is tyrosine-hydroxylase deficiency with relatively preserved norepinephrine transporter; (3) roughly one-third of patients phenoconvert, with identifiable clinical and biomarker predictors; and (4) droxidopa and midodrine are the evidence-supported, pathophysiology-matched therapies for the orthostatic hypotension.

1. Disease Information

Overview. PAF is a chronic, slowly progressive degenerative disorder of the autonomic nervous system characterized by isolated (at onset) autonomic failure in the absence of other neurological deficits. The cardinal manifestation is neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Pathologically it is defined by predominantly peripheral deposition of α-synuclein and degeneration of postganglionic sympathetic neurons (PMID: 31515103; PMID: 24095130).

"Pathologically, PAF is characterized by predominantly peripheral deposition of α-synuclein." — PMID: 31515103

"characterized by isolated peripheral autonomic dysfunction and decreased norepinephrine synthesis" — PMID: 24095130

Key identifiers. - MONDO: MONDO:0018608 - MeSH: Pure Autonomic Failure (D054970) - ICD-10: G90.3 (multi-system degeneration of the autonomic nervous system); ICD-11: autonomic nervous system disorder range - Orphanet: ORPHA:95429 (Pure autonomic failure) - OMIM: Not recorded as a Mendelian entry (sporadic disease; no causal gene registered)

Synonyms / alternative names. Bradbury–Eggleston syndrome; PAF; pure dysautonomia; pure idiopathic dysautonomia; idiopathic orthostatic hypotension.

Information source. Information is derived from aggregated disease-level resources (OMIM/Orphanet/MeSH, clinical cohort studies, autopsy series, and natural-history registries such as the Natural History Study of the Synucleinopathies and the Queen Square cohort), not single-patient EHR extraction.

2. Etiology

Primary cause. PAF is a sporadic neurodegenerative α-synucleinopathy. The proximal molecular cause is misfolding and aggregation of α-synuclein (SNCA) into β-sheet-rich fibrils forming intraneuronal Lewy bodies in peripheral autonomic neurons. No environmental trigger or infectious agent is established as causal.

Genetic risk factors. PAF occurs sporadically with no established Mendelian inheritance (PMID: 24095130: "PAF occurs sporadically"). However, rare SNCA lesions can produce a PAF-like noradrenergic/cardiac denervation phenotype, directly implicating α-synuclein dosage and structure (see Section 4). As a member of the α-synucleinopathy family, PAF likely shares susceptibility architecture (e.g., SNCA common variants, GBA variants) with PD/DLB, though PAF-specific GWAS data are lacking.

Environmental risk factors. Older age is the dominant demographic risk factor (mean onset ~63 years). A modest male predominance is observed (~64% male in large cohorts). No specific toxin, occupational exposure, or lifestyle factor has been causally linked.

Protective factors. None established genetically or environmentally for PAF specifically.

Gene–environment interactions. Not characterized for PAF. The disease is best modeled as a predominantly stochastic/age-related proteinopathy with rare monogenic (SNCA-dosage) phenocopies.

3. Phenotypes

The core phenotype is neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with multi-system autonomic failure. Autonomic failure manifests across genitourinary, bowel, and thermoregulatory domains (PMID: 31515103: "Autonomic failure may also manifest as genitourinary, bowel, and thermoregulatory dysfunction.").

Phenotype Type HPO term Onset/Severity/Course Frequency
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (dizziness, presyncope, syncope) Clinical sign / symptom HP:0004926 (Orthostatic hypotension); HP:0001278 (Syncope) Adult/late-onset; moderate–severe; progressive Universal (defining feature)
Supine hypertension Clinical sign HP:0012694 Co-occurs with nOH; variable Common (>50% of nOH patients across dysautonomias)
Erectile/sexual dysfunction, urinary urgency/retention Symptom HP:0000012 (Abnormality of the urinary system); HP:0000144 Often early; progressive Common
Constipation / bowel dysmotility Symptom HP:0002019 Progressive Common
Anhidrosis / hypohidrosis (thermoregulatory/sudomotor failure) Clinical sign HP:0000966 / HP:0000821 Progressive Common
REM sleep behavior disorder (dream enactment) Behavioral/sleep HP:0002494 Often prodromal Frequent; prodromal synucleinopathy marker

Quality-of-life impact. nOH substantially impairs daily functioning, increasing risk of falls, syncope, and functional disability; orthostatic symptoms limit upright activity. The combination of OH + RBD marks a "malignant" phenotype associated with cognitive impairment, postural instability, and reduced survival (PMID: 31142660: "The combination of OH and RBD was associated with cognitive impairment and more rapid progression of postural instability").

4. Genetic / Molecular Information

Causal gene. There is no Mendelian causal gene for sporadic PAF. The causal protein is α-synuclein (SNCA, HGNC:11138; OMIM gene 163890; chromosome 4q22.1), which is the aggregating species in all PAF neuropathology.

Rare SNCA lesions producing a PAF-like phenotype (PMID: 14736756; PMID: 31178336):

Variant Type Functional consequence Phenotype
SNCA whole-gene triplication (Iowa kindred) Copy-number / structural Gain of function via overexpression of normal α-synuclein Lewy body parkinsonism with cardiac sympathetic denervation and orthostatic hypotension
SNCA E46K Missense Aggregation-prone; aggressive Lewy body disease Can present as PAF with severe cutaneous p-synuclein and small-fiber denervation

"cardiac sympathetic denervation cosegregates with parkinsonism" … "where disease is caused by overexpression of normal alpha-synuclein" — PMID: 14736756

"All E46K-SNCA carriers had moderate to severe p-synuclein deposits and small fiber neurodegeneration" — PMID: 31178336

These establish SNCA gene dosage/structure as mechanistically sufficient to produce the cardiac noradrenergic denervation characteristic of PAF, even though sporadic PAF carries no recurrent germline mutation.

Variant classification. The triplication and E46K are pathogenic for Lewy body disease; no recurrent pathogenic variant exists for sporadic PAF. Allele frequencies of these lesions are effectively absent in gnomAD (private/family-specific).

Somatic vs germline. The SNCA lesions above are germline. Sporadic PAF is not driven by an identified somatic variant.

Modifier genes / epigenetics / chromosomal abnormalities. Not characterized specifically for PAF beyond the SNCA-dosage effect (a copy-number/structural mechanism). The SNCA triplication is itself a large-scale genomic (copy-number) abnormality.

5. Environmental Information

  • Environmental factors / toxins: None established as causal for PAF.
  • Lifestyle factors: None causally linked. Dietary salt/fluid status strongly modulates symptom severity (volume depletion worsens nOH) but is not etiologic.
  • Infectious agents: Not applicable — PAF is a degenerative proteinopathy, not an infectious or post-infectious disorder.

6. Mechanism / Pathophysiology

Ordered causal chain

  1. α-synuclein (SNCA) misfolds and aggregates into β-sheet-rich, seeding-competent fibrils in peripheral autonomic neurons (gain of toxic function) — leads to →
  2. Intraneuronal Lewy-body / Lewy-neurite inclusions form in sympathetic ganglia, intermediolateral columns of the spinal cord, and distal autonomic axons of heart and bladder — results in →
  3. Noradrenergic neuron dysfunction: tyrosine-hydroxylase (TH) depletion, impaired vesicular catecholamine storage, and postganglionic denervation — leads to →
  4. Deficient norepinephrine release at sympathetic vascular terminals (very low supine plasma NE, no orthostatic rise) — results in →
  5. Failure of baroreflex-mediated vasoconstriction on standing — leads to →
  6. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and multi-system autonomic failure (urogenital, GI, sudomotor), the clinical manifestation.
  7. Branch (in ~30% over ~6 yr): α-synuclein pathology spreads to the CNS (locus coeruleus, substantia nigra) — leads to phenoconversion to:
  8. PD / DLB — if sympathetic intraneuronal Lewy-type synucleinopathy with low NE, OR
  9. MSA — if preserved noradrenergic status (normal supine NE, intact pupils, cardiovagal responses).

Steps 1–2 (prion-like seeding/spread) are partly inferred from CSF seed-amplification assays and animal models rather than fully demonstrated in situ in living humans.

Supporting detail by category

  • Protein dysfunction: α-synuclein misfolding/aggregation (loss of normal synaptic function + toxic gain of function). CSF αSyn-PMCA is positive in ~94% of PAF, confirming seeding-competent misfolded α-synuclein (PMID: 33881777). In PAF/PD the aggregates are neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions (Lewy bodies), in contrast to the glial cytoplasmic inclusions of MSA (PMID: 24095130: "they take the form of neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions called Lewy bodies in PAF and PD").
  • Biochemical abnormality: Profound tyrosine-hydroxylase deficiency (the rate-limiting catecholamine-synthesis enzyme, tyrosine→L-DOPA) with relatively preserved norepinephrine transporter (NET) in sympathetic nerves — "normal abundance of the NE transporter (NET) protein, together with very low levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)" (PMID: 29162745). This suggests synthetic dysfunction may precede/exceed outright structural denervation.
  • Dual lesion (imaging): Cardiac sympathetic PET shows that "PAF entails moderately decreased cardiac sympathetic innervation and a substantial vesicular storage defect in residual nerves" (PMID: 32945121) — i.e., both denervation and a vesicular catecholamine storage defect.
  • Cellular processes: Neurodegeneration of noradrenergic neurons; baroreflex failure.
  • Molecular pathways / metabolic changes: Catecholamine biosynthesis pathway disrupted at the TH step (tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine → norepinephrine).

Suggested GO terms: GO:0042423 (catecholamine biosynthetic process), GO:0042136 (neurotransmitter biosynthetic process), GO:0007268 (chemical synaptic transmission), GO:0003018 (vascular process in circulatory system). GO cellular component: GO:0097413 (Lewy body); synaptic vesicle (GO:0008021). CL terms: CL:0000540 (neuron), CL:0011103 (sympathetic noradrenergic neuron / postganglionic sympathetic neuron).

7. Anatomical Structures Affected

Organ / system level. - Primary: Peripheral autonomic nervous system — sympathetic ganglia, postganglionic sympathetic nerves. Body systems: autonomic (sympathetic) nervous system; cardiovascular (blood-pressure regulation); genitourinary; gastrointestinal; integumentary (sudomotor). - Secondary (with phenoconversion): central nervous system (locus coeruleus, substantia nigra).

Autopsy-defined pathology (PMID: 9255396): cell loss in intermediolateral columns (spinal cord) and sympathetic ganglia; Lewy bodies in substantia nigra, locus coeruleus, substantia innominata, and sympathetic ganglia; and in distal autonomic axons — epicardial fat (cardiac), periadrenal adipose nerve fascicles, and nerves in the muscularis of the urinary bladder. "Sites of autonomic nerve involvement correlated with clinical symptomatology."

"histopathologically by cell loss in intermediolateral columns and sympathetic ganglia" — PMID: 9255396

"Lewy bodies in this disease may be seen in distal axons at a great length from their primary cell bodies" — PMID: 9255396

Tissue / cell level. Nervous tissue; postganglionic sympathetic noradrenergic neurons (CL:0011103). Subcellular: neuronal cytoplasm (Lewy-body inclusions; GO:0097413 Lewy body); synaptic vesicle catecholamine storage compartment (vesicular storage defect).

Localization (UBERON): UBERON:0001806 (sympathetic ganglion / paravertebral ganglion), UBERON:0002260 (intermediolateral nucleus — spinal cord lateral horn), UBERON:0000948 (heart), UBERON:0001255 (urinary bladder), UBERON:0001872 (locus coeruleus), UBERON:0002038 (substantia nigra). Lateralization: bilateral/systemic.

8. Temporal Development

  • Onset: Adult/late-onset; mean age ~63 years (63.1 yr in meta-analysis). Pattern: insidious, chronic.
  • Progression: Slowly progressive over years to decades. Disease course is chronic and progressive; nOH is often a relatively late and severe sign of autonomic degeneration. In some patients the "pure" peripheral phase is stable for many years (Queen Square median follow-up ~10 yr).
  • Critical transition / phenoconversion: ~30% convert to a central synucleinopathy over a mean of ~6.4 years (meta-analysis); independent cohorts report ~33% over ~10–13 years. This defines a critical window for prognostication and potential future neuroprotective intervention.
  • Duration: Chronic, lifelong.

9. Inheritance and Population

Epidemiology. PAF is rare (Orphanet ORPHA:95429). Precise population prevalence/incidence estimates are not well established; it is the least common of the primary chronic autonomic failure syndromes. Cohort demographics: mean onset ~63 years, male predominance ~64% (meta-analytic cohort, PMID: 42081229).

Inheritance. Sporadic / non-Mendelian (multifactorial, age-related). No inheritance pattern, penetrance, anticipation, founder effect, consanguinity role, or carrier frequency applies to sporadic PAF. The rare SNCA triplication kindred shows autosomal-dominant transmission of a Lewy body phenotype that includes PAF-like cardiac denervation, but this is a phenocopy, not sporadic PAF.

Population demographics. No specific ethnic/geographic predilection established. Sex ratio modestly male-skewed; age distribution concentrated in older adults.

10. Diagnostics

Autonomic function testing is the diagnostic cornerstone: demonstration of neurogenic OH (sustained BP fall on standing/head-up tilt with inadequate heart-rate compensation and blunted NE response).

Biomarkers and tests:

Test Finding in PAF Performance PMID
Supine plasma norepinephrine Low (often <100–200 pg/mL), no orthostatic rise Differentiates peripheral (PAF/PD) vs central (MSA) lesion 24095130, 40696849
Cutaneous p-synuclein (distal-leg skin biopsy) Present in 22/22 (100%) PAF Total p-syn score >3: 100% specificity, 82% sensitivity vs MSA 39608812
CSF αSyn-PMCA (seed amplification) Positive in ~94% of PAF Confirms α-synucleinopathy; MSA-type kinetics + NfL predict MSA conversion 33881777
¹²³I-MIBG cardiac scintigraphy Reduced/absent uptake (PAF/PD); intact in MSA "most sensitive test for early detection of autonomic dysfunction" 38216420
CSF/plasma NfL + αSyn oligomers Elevated NfL predicts conversion Prognostic 33881777
NM-MRI / FDOPA-PET Reduced LC/SN contrast in high-conversion-risk PAF Early CNS involvement biomarker 39825743

"Total p-syn score >3 distinguished PAF from MSA with 100% specificity and 82% sensitivity." — PMID: 39608812

"αSyn-PMCA is almost invariably positive in the CSF of patients with PAF establishing this condition as α-synucleinopathy." — PMID: 33881777

"MIBG myocardial scintigraphy is the most sensitive test for early detection of autonomic dysfunction." — PMID: 38216420

Genetic testing. Not routinely indicated for sporadic PAF. SNCA copy-number/sequence testing is relevant only where a strong family history of Lewy body disease suggests an SNCA-dosage phenocopy.

Differential diagnosis. MSA (preserved supine NE, intact pupils/cardiovagal responses, glial inclusions), PD/DLB with autonomic failure, dopamine-β-hydroxylase deficiency, diabetic/amyloid autonomic neuropathy, and non-neurogenic OH (volume depletion, drugs). The supine plasma NE level is a key discriminator — a normal supine NE in a PAF-like presentation is a red flag for later MSA conversion (PMID: 35790426; PMID: 40696849).

Screening. No population screening for PAF. Research-grade risk stratification of RBD patients and PAF patients identifies individuals at high prodromal risk for synucleinopathy conversion.

11. Outcome / Prognosis

PAF itself is relatively benign in its "pure" peripheral phase compared with MSA, but it carries a substantial risk of phenoconversion to a more disabling central synucleinopathy.

Phenoconversion (PMID: 42081229): In a meta-analysis of 9 studies / 900 PAF patients, 270/900 (30%) phenoconverted over mean 6.4 years — 12% to MSA, 11% to DLB, 7% to PD (pooled incidence ~5.6/100 person-years). The Queen Square cohort (n=281, median 10-yr follow-up) reported 33% conversion (PMID: 40397689).

"270 of 900 individuals with PAF (30%) experienced phenoconversion to a central α-synucleinopathy (12% to MSA, 11% to DLB, 7% to PD)" — PMID: 42081229

"Of these, 33% (91) converted to a more widespread synucleinopathy" — PMID: 40397689

Prognostic factors (PMID: 38366572; PMID: 40696849): - Faster phenoconversion associated with urinary dysfunction (HR 5.9), sexual dysfunction (HR 3.6), subtle motor signs (HR 2.7), dysphagia (HR 2.5), speech changes (HR 2.4). - Noradrenergic status bifurcates trajectory: low supine NE + Lewy bodies → PD/DLB; preserved/normal NE, normal pupils, intact cardiovagal response → MSA. Younger age + higher supine NE favor MSA. - OH + RBD "malignant" phenotype → cognitive decline, postural instability, reduced survival (PMID: 31142660).

"Faster phenoconversion from study enrolment to any diagnosis was associated with urinary and sexual dysfunction" — PMID: 38366572

Morbidity. Falls, syncope, injury, and functional disability from nOH; supine hypertension risks target-organ damage. Mortality is driven largely by the central synucleinopathy following conversion (MSA conveys the worst prognosis).

12. Treatment

Treatment is symptomatic — there is no disease-modifying therapy. Drug selection is pathophysiology-guided: because PAF has peripheral noradrenergic degeneration and low sympathetic reserve, patients respond better to norepinephrine "replacers" (midodrine, droxidopa) than to NE "enhancers" (pyridostigmine, atomoxetine), which require spared postganglionic fibers (as in MSA) (PMID: 32979782; PMID: 31996627; PMID: 33705537).

"those with peripheral noradrenergic degeneration (pure autonomic failure, Parkinson's disease) and low plasma norepinephrine, tend to respond better to 'norepinephrine replacers' (midodrine and droxidopa)" — PMID: 32979782

"Patients with peripheral sympathetic denervation respond better to norepinephrine agonists/precursors such as droxidopa" — PMID: 31996627

Non-pharmacologic (first-line): increased fluid and dietary salt, compression stockings/abdominal binders, physical counter-maneuvers, head-up sleeping, portioned meals, bolus water drinking.

Pharmacologic:

Drug Class / mechanism Evidence NCIT
Midodrine α1-adrenergic agonist (direct pressor) Approved for OH; first-line pressor NCIT:C61721
Droxidopa (L-threo-DOPS) Norepinephrine prodrug FDA-approved for nOH; 3 RCTs (see below) NCIT:C66878
Fludrocortisone Mineralocorticoid (volume expander) Adjunct; use with caution NCIT:C29082
Pyridostigmine Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (NE enhancer) Better in MSA/mild disease; less effective in PAF NCIT:C47629
Ampreloxetine Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor Phase 2 positive (emerging) —
Desmopressin Vasopressin analog (nocturnal polyuria) Caution (hyponatremia) NCIT:C61763

Droxidopa RCT evidence (PMID: 28494751; PMID: 27538531): Pooled analysis (n=460) showed droxidopa significantly reduced OHQ composite (−2.68±2.20 vs −1.82±2.34; P<0.001) and dizziness/lightheadedness, improved activities of daily living, and raised upright systolic BP (11.5±20.5 vs 4.8±21.0 mmHg; P<0.001), with low supine-hypertension rates (≤7.9% vs ≤4.6% placebo). NNT for OHSA item-1 improvement was <10.

"Droxidopa improved virtually all nOH symptom scores compared with placebo, significantly reducing OHQ composite score (−2.68 ± 2.20 vs −1.82 ± 2.34 units; P < 0.001)" — PMID: 28494751

"The NNT for droxidopa for improvement in OHSA Item 1 was <10" — PMID: 27538531

Durability caveat: Benefit is largely short-term; durability beyond weeks 1–2 was inconsistent across endpoints (PMID: 25487613; PMID: 25350981, the latter a randomized-withdrawal study that failed its primary endpoint though secondary/composite outcomes favored droxidopa).

Ampreloxetine (NRI) raised seated SBP (+29.9 mmHg vs placebo; P=0.0112) and improved symptoms in a phase 2 nOH trial (PMID: 34657222).

"Seated blood pressure increased 15.7 mmHg 4 h after ampreloxetine and decreased 14.2 mmHg after placebo" — PMID: 34657222

Key therapeutic trade-off: nOH and neurogenic supine hypertension are hemodynamically opposed — "Because nOH and nSH are hemodynamically opposed, therapies to treat one condition may exacerbate the other" (PMID: 33687577) — requiring individualized balancing (e.g., short-acting nocturnal antihypertensives, avoiding late-day pressors).

13. Prevention

  • Primary prevention: None available (no modifiable cause).
  • Secondary prevention: Early recognition of nOH and identification of high-conversion-risk patients (biomarker/clinical stratification) for enrollment in neuroprotective trials and close monitoring.
  • Tertiary prevention: Fall prevention, management of supine hypertension to limit target-organ damage, patient education on high-risk situations (heat, large meals, posture, dehydration).
  • Genetic counseling: Generally not applicable (sporadic); relevant only for rare SNCA-dosage kindreds.
  • Immunization / public-health / environmental interventions: Not applicable.

14. Other Species / Natural Disease

  • Taxonomy: Homo sapiens (NCBI:txid9606) is the species with the natural disease. No recognized spontaneous PAF-equivalent in companion animals is documented in OMIA.
  • Orthologous gene: Snca in mouse (NCBI Gene ID 20617); SNCA orthologs are conserved across vertebrates.
  • Comparative biology: α-synuclein aggregation and autonomic/cardiac sympathetic denervation mechanisms are evolutionarily conserved and modeled experimentally (see Section 15).
  • Transmission: Not applicable (non-infectious, non-zoonotic). Note the experimental "prion-like" seeding behavior of α-synuclein is a laboratory phenomenon, not natural transmission.

15. Model Organisms

Dedicated PAF mouse model (PMID: 32071315): injection of α-synuclein preformed fibrils into autonomic ganglia of human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (TgM83) mice produces α-synuclein pathology confined to the autonomic nervous system with autonomic dysfunction and NO motor features — recapitulating the "pure" peripheral phenotype.

"in the pure autonomic failure (PAF), α-synuclein (α-Syn) pathology is confined within the autonomic nervous system with no motor features, but mouse models recapitulating PAF without motor dysfunction are lacking" — PMID: 32071315

Broader rodent synucleinopathy models (PMID: 23933655): genetic and toxin-induced models reproduce cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction and sympathetic denervation that often precede motor signs:

"cardiovascular autonomic impairments including orthostatic hypotension and sympathetic denervation may precede the development of the cardinal motor symptoms" — PMID: 23933655

Human genetic "model": the SNCA-triplication kindred confirms gene-dosage causality for cardiac denervation + parkinsonism (PMID: 14736756).

Model types: mammalian (mouse — A53T TgM83, MGI resources); induced (fibril-injection, toxin). Genetic models: transgenic human α-synuclein (A53T). Recapitulation: autonomic-restricted pathology without motor involvement (good model for the "pure" peripheral phase). Limitations: phenoconversion to human-like MSA/DLB/PD subtypes and the TH-selective biochemical lesion are incompletely modeled.

Mechanistic Model / Interpretation

    SNCA (α-synuclein) misfolding & aggregation (toxic gain of function)
                   │  [CSF αSyn-PMCA + in ~94%]
                   ▼
     Lewy-body inclusions in peripheral autonomic neurons
     (sympathetic ganglia, IML columns, cardiac & bladder axons)  [autopsy: 9255396]
                   │
                   ▼
     Noradrenergic neuron dysfunction:
     ↓Tyrosine hydroxylase  +  vesicular storage defect  +  denervation
     (NET relatively preserved)              [29162745, 32945121]
                   │
                   ▼
     ↓↓ Norepinephrine release (low supine plasma NE, no orthostatic rise)
                   │
                   ▼
     Baroreflex vasoconstriction failure on standing
                   │
                   ▼
     NEUROGENIC ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION  +  urogenital/GI/sudomotor failure
                   │
                   ▼  (~30% over ~6 yr; CNS spread to LC/SN)
    ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
    ▼                                              ▼
   Low NE + Lewy type                           Preserved NE, normal pupils,
   → PD / DLB                                    intact cardiovagal → MSA
   [34669076, 40696849]                          [35790426, 40696849]

The model is internally consistent and well-supported through step 6 (clinical manifestation). The upstream seeding/spreading steps (1–2) and the CNS-spread branch (step 7) are supported by seed-amplification assays, imaging, and animal models but remain partly inferred rather than directly demonstrated in situ in living humans. Branch assignment is supported by PMID: 34669076: "the form of PAF that involves sympathetic intraneuronal synucleinopathy and noradrenergic deficiency can phenoconvert to PD or DLB-but not to MSA."

Limitations and Knowledge Gaps

  1. No PAF-specific genetics/GWAS. Susceptibility architecture is inferred from the broader α-synucleinopathy family; no PAF-specific common-variant or modifier-gene data exist.
  2. Prevalence/incidence are poorly quantified. PAF is rare and often reclassified upon phenoconversion, confounding epidemiologic estimates.
  3. Upstream mechanism partly inferred. Prion-like seeding and spread (steps 1–2, 7) rely on seed-amplification assays and animal models, not direct in vivo human demonstration.
  4. Treatment durability uncertain. Droxidopa's long-term efficacy is inconsistent; one randomized-withdrawal trial failed its primary endpoint (PMID: 25350981). Most PAF-specific treatment data derive from mixed nOH cohorts rather than PAF-only trials.
  5. No disease-modifying therapy. Nothing yet alters phenoconversion risk or α-synuclein accumulation.
  6. Conversion prediction imperfect. Biomarkers improve but do not perfectly predict which patients convert or to which subtype.

Proposed Follow-up Experiments / Actions

  1. Prospective biomarker-stratified cohort combining supine plasma NE, pupillometry, cardiovagal responses, CSF αSyn-PMCA kinetics, NfL, and NM-MRI/FDOPA-PET to build a validated conversion-risk calculator (building on PMID: 40696849, 39825743).
  2. Neuroprotective trials in high-risk PAF — target the prodromal window using α-synuclein–directed agents (immunotherapy, aggregation inhibitors) with phenoconversion as the endpoint.
  3. PAF-only pragmatic treatment trials of droxidopa vs midodrine vs ampreloxetine with durability (≥6-month) and supine-hypertension co-endpoints.
  4. Mechanistic work on the TH-selective lesion (PMID: 29162745) — determine whether restoring catecholamine synthesis (e.g., optimized L-DOPS dosing, TH cofactor support) rescues function before structural denervation is complete.
  5. Refine the TgM83 ganglionic-fibril model (PMID: 32071315) to model phenoconversion branches and test anti-spreading therapeutics.
  6. Harmonize diagnostic criteria to incorporate skin p-synuclein, seed amplification, and MIBG, and prospectively validate against autopsy (extending PMID: 42444112).

Report compiled from 11 confirmed findings and 37 reviewed papers. Evidence source types span human clinical (cohorts, RCTs, autopsy), model organism (transgenic/fibril mouse, rodent), in vitro/ex vivo (skin biopsy, CSF seed amplification), and imaging.
